The early life stages of Microcondylaea bonellii are characterized by a brief embryonic phase. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the period from egg fertilization to the emergence of the first free-swimming larva lasts approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. Upon hatching, the newly released glochidium larva possesses a minute shell, measuring only 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm] in length at birth. This parasitic larval stage must attach to the gills or fins of a suitable fish host to continue its development. Following a period of encystment and metamorphosis on the host, the larva excysts and settles onto the riverbed substrate as a juvenile. The shell length at settlement is remarkably small, recorded at just 0.03 cm . This phase represents a critical transition from a parasitic to a free-living benthic existence. The size at which these events occur is highly consistent within populations, reflecting a tightly regulated developmental program that has evolved to maximize the probability of successful recruitment in the dynamic lotic environments typical of this unionid species. Post-settlement growth proceeds rapidly under favorable conditions.

As the juvenile bivalve matures, its growth trajectory follows a pattern typical of many freshwater unionids. Longitudinal field studies have demonstrated that the shell length at the onset of sexual maturity is consistently near 3.5 cm [Lp = consistently near 3.5 cm]. This threshold is typically reached after approximately 4 to 5 years of growth, depending on local environmental conditions such as food availability and water temperature. The attainment of this size marks the commencement of gametogenesis and the ability to participate in reproductive activities. Once individuals surpass this pubertal size, they enter into the reproductively active adult phase of their life history. The ultimate shell length attained by fully grown adults is approximately 8.5 cm [Li = approximately 8.5 cm], a value that appears to represent the maximum size achievable under optimal environmental conditions. Specimens approaching this maximum dimension are relatively rare in natural populations, likely due to the cumulative stresses of senescence and predation over many years. This size is consistent with that of other European unionids inhabiting comparable river systems, suggesting a conserved allometric relationship.

The maximum potential lifespan of Microcondylaea bonellii is considerable for a freshwater bivalve. When maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], individuals in stable, low-stress environments have been documented to survive for up to 60 years [am = up to 60 years]. This extraordinary longevity implies a very slow rate of physiological aging and a life-history strategy heavily invested in persistence. Achieving such a long life requires efficient energy management and robust cellular maintenance mechanisms. In terms of body mass, an individual reaching the ultimate shell length of 8.5 cm attains a corresponding maximum wet weight of approximately 22.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 22.1 grams]. This mass, which represents the heaviest point in the animal's life, is achieved only after several decades of sustained somatic growth. The relationship between shell length and wet weight in this species follows a typical cubic allometry, meaning that the largest individuals are disproportionately heavy compared to their length. This substantial body mass provides a large tissue volume for metabolic and reproductive activities.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial but concentrated within discrete periods. At the standard reference temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a mature female can produce, on average, approximately 274 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 274 offspring per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This daily rate of glochidial release is critical for ensuring that a sufficient number of larvae encounter a suitable host fish. The total annual reproductive effort is therefore immense, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over parental investment in individual offspring. This maximum reproduction rate appears to be constrained by the energetic demands of both gamete production and the metabolic costs of the adult itself. The production of such a large number of propagules places a significant physiological burden on the female, particularly in terms of resource investment in the developing eggs. Environmental factors that influence the female's condition, such as food availability and water quality, directly impact this reproductive capacity.

Comparative data from related unionid species provide context for the life-history traits of Microcondylaea bonellii. The documented maximum lifespan of 60 years [am = 60 years] places this species among the longer-lived members of its family, rivaling the longevity of some larger Margaritifera species at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Similarly, its ultimate wet weight of 22.1 grams [Wwi = 22.1 grams] is substantial for a bivalve of its shell dimensions, suggesting a relatively heavy tissue-to-shell ratio. The shell length at puberty of 3.5 cm [Lp = 3.5 cm] represents a size-based threshold for reproductive competence that is common among European freshwater mussels. The remarkably small size at birth and settlement, 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm] and 0.03 cm  respectively, underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early life stages and the strong selective pressure for high fecundity. The daily reproductive rate at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] reaches 274 offspring per day [Ri = 274 offspring per day], which is consistent with a parasitic larval strategy requiring many propagules to ensure host encounter. The age at birth of 10 days [ab = 10 days] is a short developmental period, characteristic of species with an obligate parasitic phase at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Finally, the ultimate shell length of 8.5 cm [Li = 8.5 cm] is a common adult size for this genus in European watercourses.
